name: Bagerhat
tagline: A medieval mosque-city carved out of the mangroves — the seventy-seven domes of Khan Jahan Ali's great masjid, a UNESCO World Heritage ensemble, and the Sundarbans along the district's southern edge.

guide.bestTime: October to March — dry, cool and comfortable for the open monument sites, and the right season for Sundarbans boat trips from Mongla.
guide.gettingThere: By road from Khulna (~35 km, ~1 hr) or from Dhaka (~roughly 4–5 hr via the Padma Bridge). Bagerhat town has no passenger railway — the nearest is Khulna — and the Sundarbans is reached by boat from Mongla in the south of the district.
guide.difficulty: Easy for the mosque city, whose monuments sit in two clusters a few kilometres apart on flat ground; moderate for the Sundarbans, which means a boat trip and a full day or more.

mustVisit.name: Sixty Dome Mosque (Shat Gombuj Masjid)
mustVisit.description: The crown of the World Heritage city and the largest medieval mosque in Bangladesh — a vast brick prayer hall roofed with dome upon dome, raised on a forest of stone pillars.
mustVisit.history: Built by Khan Jahan Ali around 1440–1459, the mosque actually carries 77 domes (including seven curved chau-chala vaults over the central aisle) supported by 60 stone pillars — and it is from those sixty pillars, not the domes, that its 'sixty' name is thought to come.

practical.hours: Daytime; closed on the weekly off-day

howToReach.fromDistrictTown: On the Khulna–Bagerhat road, ~6 km west of Bagerhat town
howToReach.transport: Bus, CNG or auto from town or Khulna

mustVisit.bestTime: Cool, dry months; mornings for the light and fewer crowds
tips: Dress modestly — it is an active mosque as well as a monument
The little site museum nearby helps make sense of the mosque city

mustVisit.name: Tomb of Khan Jahan Ali & Thakur Dighi
mustVisit.description: The mausoleum of the saint-general who founded the city, on the bank of the great Thakur Dighi tank — a place of pilgrimage whose waters are famously home to crocodiles.
mustVisit.history: Khan Jahan Ali, who carved the medieval city of Khalifatabad out of the mangroves, died in 1459 and was buried here. Folklore links the crocodiles of Thakur Dighi to the two he is said to have ridden; the shrine still draws pilgrims from across the country.

howToReach.fromDistrictTown: Eastern (mausoleum) zone, ~6 km from the Sixty Dome Mosque

tips: Be respectful — it is an active shrine
Keep a safe distance from the tank's edge where the crocodiles are

mustVisit.name: Nine Dome Mosque (Noy Gombuj Masjid)
mustVisit.description: A graceful nine-domed mosque just west of Thakur Dighi — one central dome ringed by eight others — close to Khan Jahan Ali's tomb.
mustVisit.history: Part of the 15th-century Khan-e-Jahan-style ensemble, the Nine Dome Mosque is among the best preserved of the smaller monuments in the eastern zone of the mosque city.

howToReach.fromDistrictTown: West bank of Thakur Dighi, near the tomb
howToReach.transport: Walk from the tomb, or CNG from town

tips: Easy to pair with the tomb right beside it

mustVisit.name: Ronvijoypur Mosque
mustVisit.description: A single-domed 15th-century mosque crowned by the largest dome of any mosque in Bangladesh — a thick-walled, sturdy hall near the Khulna–Bagerhat road.
mustVisit.history: Another of Khan Jahan Ali's works, Ronvijoypur is famed for its enormous single dome (about 11 metres across), set on massively thick brick walls in the Khan-e-Jahan style.

howToReach.fromDistrictTown: Near the Khulna–Bagerhat road, between the two monument zones

tips: Step inside to feel the scale of the single great dome
Combine with the other monuments along the road

mustVisit.name: The Lesser Mosques of the Mosque City
mustVisit.description: Scattered among the rice fields and villages around the city are the smaller jewels of the ensemble — Singair, Bibi Begni and Chunakhola mosques — each a single-domed 15th-century gem.
mustVisit.history: The medieval city once held hundreds of mosques and structures. Singair stands beside the Sixty Dome Mosque, Bibi Begni and Chunakhola sit out among the fields to the west — all part of the UNESCO-listed Khan-e-Jahan-style ensemble.

howToReach.fromDistrictTown: Around the western (mosque) zone, near the Sixty Dome Mosque
howToReach.transport: CNG or auto; some need a short walk through the fields

tips: Chunakhola and Bibi Begni reward a short walk through the rice fields
A local guide can string the scattered mosques into one circuit

mustVisit.name: Kodla Math (Ayodhya Math)
mustVisit.description: A tall, slender terracotta Hindu temple tower rising above Ayodhya village — a striking contrast to the domed mosques, and a reminder of the district's older religious layers.
mustVisit.history: Kodla Math is a tower-style temple ('math') decorated with terracotta, standing in Ayodhya village a short way from Bagerhat town. It is a Hindu monument quite distinct from the Islamic World Heritage ensemble.

howToReach.fromDistrictTown: Ayodhya village, ~10 km from Bagerhat town

tips: Look closely at the terracotta ornament on the tower
A good counterpoint to a day among the mosques

mustVisit.name: The Sundarbans via Mongla & Karamjal
mustVisit.description: The world's largest mangrove forest reaches into the south of the district — entered by boat from the port town of Mongla, with the Karamjal centre a popular first taste of the tidal jungle.
mustVisit.history: Mongla, on the Pasur river, is Bangladesh's second-largest seaport and the main gateway to the Sundarbans. Boats from here reach forest stations such as Karamjal and Harbaria, where spotted deer, crocodiles, monkeys — and, rarely, the Royal Bengal tiger — inhabit the mangroves.

practical.hours: Daytime boat trips; longer tours run overnight on boats
practical.entryFee: Forest entry fees and boat hire; permits required for deeper areas

howToReach.fromDistrictTown: Mongla is in the south of the district; boats to Karamjal from Mongla
howToReach.transport: Bus/car to Mongla, then engine-boat into the forest

mustVisit.bestTime: Cool, dry months for comfortable boating and wildlife
tips: Arrange a registered boat and guide; permits are required for the reserve
Karamjal is an easy half-day; Harbaria and beyond need a longer trip
Carry water, sun protection and insect repellent

specialties.name: Golda Chingri (Giant Freshwater Prawn)
specialties.description: Shrimp and prawn farming is the lifeblood of the district — the ghers of Rampal, Mongla and Fakirhat help make greater Khulna the heart of Bangladesh's shrimp country, and golda chingri is the prize of the local table.
specialties.venue: Local markets and restaurants across the district

specialties.name: Khejur Gur (Date-Palm Jaggery)
specialties.description: The greater Khulna region is renowned for its date-palm jaggery — sap tapped on cold winter nights and boiled to fragrant nolen gur, the base of the season's pithas and sweets.
specialties.venue: Winter village markets across the region

famousPeople.name: Khan Jahan Ali
famousPeople.knownFor: The 15th-century saint-administrator who founded the medieval city of Khalifatabad (Bagerhat), building the Sixty Dome Mosque and reputedly hundreds of mosques, tanks and roads carved out of the mangroves. Of Central Asian origin, he came to Bengal and governed here until his death in 1459; his tomb remains a place of pilgrimage.

didYouKnow: The Historic Mosque City of Bagerhat became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1985 — among Bangladesh's first inscriptions, alongside the Sundarbans and Paharpur.
Despite being called the 'Sixty Dome Mosque', it actually has 77 domes — the name is thought to come from its 60 stone pillars.
The medieval city of Khalifatabad was carved out of the Sundarbans mangroves in the 15th century by Khan Jahan Ali, who is said to have built around 360 mosques and structures.
Ronvijoypur Mosque holds the largest single dome of any mosque in Bangladesh, about 11 metres across.

Khan Jahan Ali's great tank, Thakur Dighi, is home to crocodiles — folklore links them to the two he is said to have ridden — and Mongla in the south of the district is the country's second-largest seaport and the main gateway to the Sundarbans.
